claim.precise: Psalm 22:2 predicted three hours of darkness at Calvary, fulfilled in Matthew 27:45.
claim.scope_notes: The psalm contrasts unanswered prayer by day and night. It neither describes daytime darkness nor specifies three hours.

context.summary: The psalmist says he cries by day without answer and by night without rest, expressing continuous lament. Matthew says darkness covered the land from noon until three during the crucifixion.

strongest_case.summary: Matthew's passion is saturated with Psalm 22, and darkness accompanies the moment when Jesus soon quotes its opening. Within that deliberate literary setting, readers may connect the psalm's day-and-night language with supernatural darkness at the cross.
reasoning: Day and night provide a darkness motif.
The crucifixion scene gives the lament a vivid narrative setting.

critical_case.summary: Psalm 22:2 says the sufferer prays both during the day and during the night; it does not say night falls during daytime. It gives no duration. Matthew 27:45 supplies both the darkness and its three-hour span without citing this verse. The claimed prediction depends on replacing the verse's ordinary contrast with a different event.
reasoning: Night is a time of prayer, not an event at noon.
Three hours appears nowhere in the psalm.

verdict.summary: Psalm 22:2 describes ceaseless prayer by day and night. It does not predict darkness at Calvary or a three-hour duration; those details come entirely from Matthew.

sources.title: Language, meaning, sense and reference: Matthew's passion narrative and Psalm 22
sources.author: Andries van Aarde
sources.notes: Supports broad narrative influence without identifying verse 2 as a darkness prediction.

sources.title: The Relationship Between Psalm 22 and the Passion Narrative
sources.author: Harvey D. Lange
sources.notes: Does not list verse 2 as the source of the darkness.

objections.objection: The wider Psalm 22 setting could support an implicit darkness motif.
objections.reason: The strongest case includes this possibility while distinguishing it from a three-hour prediction.

objections.objection: Absence of citation does not disprove implicit allusion.
objections.reason: The verdict rests on absent content, not silence alone.

objections.objection: Fulfilment need not reproduce every detail in advance.
objections.reason: The conclusion is narrowly that this verse does not predict the claimed duration or event.

publication_copy.title: Darkness for three hours?
publication_copy.scripture_excerpt: I cry out by day … and by night, but I have no rest.

website.description: Did Psalm 22 predict three hours of darkness at Calvary?
website.summary: The psalm describes prayer by day and night; it says nothing about daytime darkness or three hours.
website.christian_case: Matthew's crucifixion account deliberately uses Psalm 22, and its darkness immediately precedes Jesus quoting the psalm's opening cry.
website.critical_case: Verse 2 simply says the sufferer prays continually—by day and by night. Matthew alone supplies darkness from noon until three and never connects it with this line.
website.verdict_label: The detail is not in the psalm
website.verdict: Psalm 22 shaped Matthew's passion story, but verse 2 does not predict the three-hour darkness. This particular list item misreads its day-and-night contrast.

carousel.heading: Did Psalm 22 predict Calvary’s darkness?
carousel.body: The psalmist cries to God by day and by night. Matthew reports three hours of darkness during the crucifixion.

carousel.heading: The wider Psalm 22 link is real
carousel.body: Matthew uses the psalm repeatedly, and Jesus quotes its opening immediately after the darkness.

carousel.heading: But verse 2 predicts no darkness
carousel.body: It describes constant prayer by day and night. The three hours come entirely from Matthew.
